mcqs.question: What's the core fix for chronic alert fatigue, beyond telling the engineer to tune it out?
options: Alert on user-facing symptoms rather than internal causes, and raise thresholds or remove alerts where noise correlates with no real impact
Tell the on-call engineer to mute notifications during off-hours
Increase every alert threshold by a fixed percentage across the board
Remove all alerts and rely entirely on manual dashboard checks
mcqs.explanation: Fixing alert fatigue means fixing what's being alerted on, not muting the person or blanket-adjusting thresholds. A flat percentage bump doesn't distinguish good alerts from bad ones, and removing all alerts trades noise for zero detection.

mcqs.question: An on-call engineer gets paged 8 times overnight for "disk usage above 80%," which is normal steady-state behavior for this service. What's the correct fix?
options: Tune the disk-usage threshold up by 5% to reduce how often it fires
Escalate every disk-usage page to a senior engineer instead of the regular on-call rotation
Remove the alert entirely, or move it to a non-paging dashboard, since 80% disk usage is normal here and requires no action
Increase disk capacity so the service never reaches 80% usage
mcqs.explanation: A small threshold bump just delays the same non-actionable noise rather than eliminating it — the metric itself was never worth paging on for this service. Escalating to someone more senior doesn't change that nothing needs fixing, and adding capacity doesn't address the alert design flaw.

mcqs.question: You've cut alert volume in half. How do you verify you didn't also cut a genuinely useful signal?
options: Ask the on-call engineer whether they feel less overwhelmed
Assume the cut was safe if no one complains within a week
Re-read the alert definitions to confirm they still look reasonable on paper
Review incidents retroactively for the following month and check whether any would have been caught earlier by a removed alert
mcqs.explanation: Comparing the cut against actual subsequent incidents is the only concrete test of whether real signal was lost — a feeling of reduced overwhelm, silence, or a paper re-read don't verify anything about missed detection.

mcqs.question: Why is silencing or deprioritizing a batch of alerts wholesale the wrong response to an overwhelmed on-call engineer?
options: Muting noisy alerts always directly improves system reliability
Silencing alerts wholesale, without fixing what they alert on, just changes which failures go unnoticed — potentially hiding a real signal in the noise
Alert fatigue can only be solved by hiring more on-call engineers
Deprioritizing alerts carries no risk as long as the engineer agrees to it
mcqs.explanation: A wholesale mute doesn't distinguish noise from the rare real signal buried in it — you might silence exactly the alert that would have caught a genuine outage. It doesn't improve reliability by itself, isn't solved purely by headcount, and the engineer's agreement doesn't remove the underlying detection risk.
